utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We are back here now today and we are starting with the Defence in earnest. We have before us a motion -- I see Ms. Residovic is not getting the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, we did not have the translation straight away, but it is all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances, first, for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry and Mr. Turone. We have a new case manager to assist us at the bar table now, Ms. Udo, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Could we have the appearances on the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. My name is Edina Residovic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic attorney from Croatia appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic along with Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are still having a problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We are hearing a terrible noise in our headphones and all the languages are mixing in together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Cynthia McMurrey and I represent Esad Landzo. It is my pleasure to introduce to you new co-counsel, Nancy Boler, who will also be representing Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am sorry, I might have anticipated things much earlier when I started talking on the question of the motion which we have before us. We have a motion before us brought by the Prosecution seeking an order for appearance of Defence witnesses and the order of cross-examination by the Prosecution and counsel for the accused. We have already had reactions to this motion by the Defence. The Trial Chamber has tried to accommodate it and we find that we do not intend to call on the Defence in respect of the first part, that is, an order of appearance of the first witnesses. We think it will not be necessary for the Defence to argue that issue. We would call on the Prosecution to move the second part, which is the order for cross-examination and we would now like to hear Mr. Niemann argue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just seek a point of clarification; did you say you did not wish to hear us in relation to the first part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, because we do not think it is really necessary in relation to the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to the second part, we, in large measure, rely on our written submission of the matter. Your Honours, the submission that we make in relation to this is that it is more a common-sense issue than anything else, because we submit that the role of cross-examination of the Prosecution is something that can be quite distinct and separate from that of the accused. I do not suggest anything sinister or wrong in this, but what I am saying is that there are often many issues which the Defence have in common and those issues can be -- because cross-examination is at large and not restricted to merely that which arose in the course of evidence-in-chief, there is a considerable opportunity available to the Defence to introduce new material in the course of cross-examination. When I say "new material", it does not have to be in the form of written exhibits or anything of that nature; it could be new material elicited through the process of questioning. In our respectful submission, this has an unfair advantage on the Prosecution, because what can happen is that the Prosecution, if it has to go first, cross-examines on the material that has been raised in evidence-in-chief and deals with that and it may deal with other wider issues as well, because, as I said, cross-examination is at large, but it deals with the ambit of matters that primarily are raised in evidence-in-chief. If then what happens is that a series of co-accused counsel then proceed to cross-examination, the potential to raise a whole lot of new matters is very considerable. If that happens, the Prosecution is left in a position where it either must apply to your Honours to further cross-examine, because of this new material, or, alternatively, it is left in a situation where it is unable to address matters which have been raised. If it is left in a situation where it cannot address them, it has to do it in a process either by way of a rebuttal case -- and that in itself may be difficult because it has not had a chance to confront the witness and, indeed, it may even be unfair to the witness, because in a situation where the Prosecution is not able to confront the witness with an issue because it cannot cross-examine, it then has to deal with it in rebuttal, and we have never heard the witness's view of the matter, which may resolve it and may preclude it. It is really just a practical common-sense question, in my respectful submission, because we do not share the same interests that the accused do. I am not saying that they are totally ad idem on all points -- that is obviously not the case -- but they have a much greater potential to do that. This is the reason why your Honours are in a situation to say to them, during the course of the Prosecution case, "Counsel will determine the order that they are going to take cross-examination" and they go off, and have very successfully and with great cooperation been able to determine the order of cross-examination, and come back and present that to your Honours -- I think, in all cases -- I do not recall one instance where there was in fact a dispute that was left to your Honours to resolve. But it potentially existed, that your Honours may have had to decide that issue where the Defence come back and say, "We cannot resolve this and we must call upon your Honours to assist us by making a decision on that." That in itself, in my respectful submission, demonstrates clearly your Honours' capacity to do this, because, if the co-accused could not agree amongst themselves, obviously you would have to decide it. Likewise, it is no different to your capacity to order the order of cross-examination vis-à-vis the co-accused Defence counsel and the Prosecution. Clearly, your Honours can do that -- you can do it in the interests of a fair trial, you can do it in the interests of an orderly trial. In my respectful submission, it does touch very much upon the issues of a fair trial, because if the Prosecution is unable to address these additional issues, which I do expect to arise, then they are going to be left dangling, as it were, and can only be resolved by rebuttal and that may not be a fair way of dealing with it, because, as your Honours are aware, one of the objects of cross-examination is to confront the witness with the issues that are raised. For that reason, it is our submission that the most effective resolution of this problem is to allow the Defence to determine amongst themselves the order of cross-examination in the way that they did it during the Prosecution case, and I am very optimistic they will be able to reach agreement on that, and then, finally, to allow the Prosecution to cross-examine at the end of all their cross-examinations. I genuinely submit to your Honour that this would be a much more efficient process and will avoid multiple applications for reopening cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I say a few things? I am sure you have seen the Defence response and the argument which you just presented has been offered in just the opposite way. This is a paragraph in the Defence response. Supposing the cross-examination by the Prosecution a witness makes a statement which is damaging to the other co-accused who, if your prayer is accepted, have already exhausted their right to cross-examination. Should that statement remain unchallenged? It is your argument, but just put the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is some truth in that, but the potential for it to happen in relation to the Prosecution is far greater. My emphasis and the difference that distinguishes us from the Defence is that it is obvious they have many more things in common than we have with them, so the potential is much greater for differences between what the Prosecution has to deal with than what the co-accused do. So, it is my submission that it is really a balancing act -- it is a question of looking at it and saying, from a common-sense perspective, what is more likely to create a situation where a party seeks to further cross-examine because an issue has arisen. For example, if you have evidence-in-chief which commences, and then the first cross-examination by a Defence counsel raises a new issue, there is no reason why that cannot be dealt with by the next counsel and so on down the line until you get to the end. It is possible, and I am not denying that, I see that it can work both ways, but it is a question of balance. It is a question of saying: where is it most likely to create difficulty? I am saying that it is on the Prosecution side, because there is no commonality of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If such a situation arises, maybe the accused, who has so suffered on account of new material being brought by the witness against him, should be given the right to further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That may happen. I think we have to be sensible. I can imagine if it is a sensibly-based request on a totally new issue that has come up and the Defence says: look, we want to re-cross-examine on this, because it has taken us by surprise, I would be hard pressed to turn around and say no, they should not be given that right. I can imagine, in those circumstances, that it would be an exceptional case, I think, for us to be opposing that. What I can see is that it is less likely for them to be doing it, because of their commonality interest, than we. It may happen in almost every case, because I anticipate genuinely to see a whole lot of new issues raised through the process of cross-examination, and we are just going to be confronted with it, so it is a practical, common-sense thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If your motion is allowed, it will have to be subject to this reservation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before you sit down, I think the misapprehension is that there can be no right to further examination by counsel -- there is such a right. There is such a right where any new material has been raised in cross-examination, the person who could be prejudiced by leaving such a matter at large, would be entitled to further cross-examination on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I perceive that from the response from the Defence that somehow or other it was suggested that we were denying that, in any circumstances, there is no right of re-cross-examination. That is not our position. I say that -- our position clearly is that, if new matters arise and it would otherwise cause prejudice, clearly there is a right of re-cross-examination, in our respectful submission, subject to the order of the court, obviously, in all cases. But, we are not trying to deny that. All we are saying is that, if the Defence go first, our applications are going to be much more restricted and it is going to be much easier to argue that, if we did not deal with it, we should have. The other way around, I suspect it will just prolong the process. Unless there are any other matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any reaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, I will make my submissions from here and not from the podium. Your Honours, I wish to address you on behalf of Mr. Delalic in response to this matter and my submissions will be brief and in support of the jointly filed motion by Delalic and Delic. We invite your Honours to reject the request by the Prosecution and to order that, after examination-in-chief of a witness is completed, the Prosecution should complete its cross-examination before co-counsel for the co-accused examine the witness. Let me begin by responding briefly to Mr. Niemann. With all due respect to my learned friend, who was not here at the beginning of this trial, we know if order of cross-examination by the Defence was not agreed upon, we followed the indictment order and that is why it worked smoothly, I think. I reject the fact that he claims that there is commonality between the co-accused necessarily -- that is obviously a supposition which cannot be founded in any kind of a joint trial. We rely on Article 21(4)(e) of the Statute, which guarantees the right of cross-examination to the accused person. Your Honours, it is only after the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination by the Prosecution that a co-accused will know whether the witness has become adverse to him or has implicated him. It is at that point that the co-accused's right under Article 21(4)(e) is triggered. The co-accused must not be precluded of that right. Our request is grounded in Article 21(4)(e). The way to ensure the full protection of the right to cross-examine of the co-accused is to hear examination-in-chief and then the

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So, we say that, contrary to the Prosecution, who is not relying on any Rule whatsoever, the Statute clearly contemplates our position, examination-in-chief followed by the Prosecution and then the co-accused should know whether or not they have an interest in cross-examining that witness. There is discretion there if the Prosecution thinks they have to reopen, but we say our request is grounded in Article 21(4)(e). There is nothing more to add. We have stated our position in our response to the Prosecution. Unless you have any further questions of me, I have no further submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am assuming here that you have taken the position that the accused person, apart from giving evidence, also calls witnesses. There are two situations -- either he is the only witness, or, in addition to him, there could be other witnesses. It depends on the position you are taking -- whether, in any event, he is the only witness, the position you are taking was to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct; I am addressing you on the order of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree; it depends on what type of case you present, whether he is the only witness, or he also calls witnesses in addition to his own evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I do not see two situations where the order of cross-examination would change, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It could always be the same, whether he calls witnesses in addition to his evidence, or whether he alone gives evidence, or even if he decides not to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We say the Prosecution should go first in cross-examination, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am only giving you the different alternatives open to an accused person. He may not even give evidence if he does not want to. He may alone give evidence, or in addition he may call other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: A couple of thoughts and I will sit down. I think Judge Jan hit it right on the head -- any argument I make will be the same argument Mr. Niemann makes. Let me suggest this: the first thing is that Rule 82(A) provides essentially that we are not having one trial here -- we have four separate trials at the same time at the same place. We are all guaranteed, as defendants, the same rights we would have in an individual trial. The procedure I am used to is that, in a multiple defendant trial, first the Prosecutor cross-examines, then the defendants cross-examine, and then the Prosecutor is allowed to re-examine on new issues -- limited to those new issues. As a practical matter, because the arguments are the same, I think that adopting that kind of procedure would probably be just as efficient as any other way around. The other thought I have is that the Statute is full of rights of the accused and the most important right for the accused, aside from the right to counsel, I think is the right to confront and cross-examine the witnesses against him. Frankly, picking a witness off the witness list that was filed today, I have no idea what a lot of those witnesses are going to say and I have absolutely no idea whether Mr. Niemann has a file folder full of statements those people made that would incriminate my client. I cannot know whether he is a witness against my client --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is talking about the reservation, if during the cross-examination by the Prosecutor, a witness says something that is damaging to another accused, he should have the right to further cross-examine him. That will be of greater advantage to you coming at the end -- with the further right to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One thing the court has to remember is that, presumably, the lawyers know their cases better than the court does at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You know your case much better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: At this point, I sincerely hope so. What I may think may be incriminatory of my client, Mr. Niemann may disagree with, or you may disagree with, because I may know something that is coming later. That is the problem I can see developing, that there may be some question about whether or not this witness, Witness A, is a witness against my client. My client's name may never come up, but it may be something that is, in my opinion, knowing more about the case, inculpatory of my client. With those few thoughts, unless the court has any questions, I am going to sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall be very brief in presenting my arguments in response to what we have heard from the Prosecution. In our written response, we opposed the motion and we abide by that, that we request that both be rejected, but my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, conscious in the absence of a precedent in terms of Rules of Procedure, in order to support his thesis, he uses logic and common-sense. This thesis cannot be acceptable for the simple reason that it proceeds from the presumption of the accused's guilt, which is impermissible. This Tribunal is both competent and qualified to judge itself the course that the proceedings are taking. Therefore, we would like to abide by our motion. We consider that the Prosecution's motion is unacceptable, and that both the proposals should be rejected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we also would like to join in Mr. O'Sullivan's arguments on the point about cross-examination. Furthermore, Mr. Moran had explained that we know a little bit more about what to expect in the witnesses, as the four cases are developed, as we go along. It might not be perceived by the court or the Prosecution that we would need to re-cross-examine, which would force us all to recall these witnesses at a later time, because of the misunderstanding about what was inculpatory at that time. I think, in the interest of the proceedings and the expeditious procession of this case, that we should be able to cross-examine after the Prosecution. Furthermore, under Article 21, when we are arguing the flip side of what Mr. Niemann is arguing, of course he has the equal right, if new material is presented to re-cross-examine, if the court so deems that it is proper at that point. When there is a tie as far as whose rights might be affected, Article 21 and all the presumptions under the Statute would say that the tie should go to the defendant and the accused. At that point, we believe that, since it is almost equal right now, that the presumption should go to the accused and we should be allowed to cross-examine after the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So you are tossing a coin, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you toss the coin, it should fall on the side of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In respect of each of the four accused, the main opposite party is the Prosecution. The Prosecution should have the right to last cross-examination then in respect of each of the four accused. If a witness makes a statement which is detrimental to the interests of any of the other accused, you said they would be given the right to further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your statement that the main opponent in this trial is the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In respect of each of the four accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We filed a motion for severance early on in January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In respect of each of the four accused -- not collectively -- in respect of each of the four accused the main opposing party is the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That should be the fact, but because it appears we will have inconsistent defences as we go along, it is not only the opposition party that is the Prosecution, but it could possibly be the other testimony of the other witnesses, so therefore I believe that during these adversarial proceedings that the defendant should have the right to cross-examine after the Prosecution, because we may not have consistent Defences during the rest of the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will adjourn and come back at 12 o'clock and give our ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have a short ruling. We rely entirely on all you have said here and our consideration of the case as a whole. The motion filed on 18 March 1998 has sought leave for an order of (a) appearance of the Defence witnesses; and (b) the order of cross-examination by the Prosecution and counsel for the accused. All counsel for the accused have opposed the motion in writing. The motion has come up for argument this morning, but, when it came up, the Trial Chamber considered it unnecessary to hear argument on the first part of the motion, namely, calling on the Trial Chamber to determine the order of appearance of the Defence witnesses. We considered that it was reasonably self-evident. The Prosecution has considered, and we agree, that the matter is not directly governed by the Statute of the Tribunal or the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. However, reliance on the practice of some common law jurisdictions, such as England and Wales, Nigeria, South Africa and Canada informs that the better practice is that where the accused gives evidence and calls witnesses, he should first give his testimony before calling his own witnesses. We agree with the view of the Defence that the proposition relied upon by the Prosecution will offend against the provisions of Article 20, which enjoins us with issues of trial and 21(4)(d), which entrenches a quality of arms in the conduct of the case between the Prosecution and the Defence. The strong implication in Rule 85(A), which enables an accused to give evidence and to call witnesses, is that the accused, by Rule 85(C), is not compellable and cannot be compelled to appear as a witness in his own Defence. Accordingly, the order in which the Defence gives evidence and calls evidence is entirely an arrangement between him and his counsel, if any. The Trial Chamber cannot interfere. In the opinion of the Trial Chamber, this is consistent with the provisions of Article 21(4)(d) and accords with the justice and fairness of a trial. It will be against the interests of justice for the Trial Chamber to determine an order when a witness is to testify and probably who the witness is. The accused is obliged to answer the charges against him to the best of his ability in his own way. I will come to the second part. The Prosecution seeks an order to cross-examine the witness of the Defence after the Defence has examined in chief, and the co-accused have cross-examined the witnesses. The Defence object to this arrangement on the ground that the Prosecution's cross-examination may reveal circumstances in the case of an accused which may affect their case. Again, facts may arise from cross-examination which may require further cross-examination. This may be lost to accused persons if the order were to be granted. It is elementary to appreciate that the case now being presented is part of the case of the Defence. The question of joint Defence apart, the Prosecutor is facing the case of the Defence. It is therefore understandable that each accused is first to examine the accused person who testifies. At the end of the cross-examination of the accused persons, the Prosecution may cross-examine. The Prosecution is entitled to speak last. There is no statutory provision in our Rules, but, fortunately, we have Section 190 of Nigerian Evidence Law, which makes such a provision in purely identical terms and I quote: "Where more than one accused is charged at the same time, a witness called by one accused may be cross-examined by the other accused and, if cross-examined by the other accused, such cross-examination shall take place before cross-examination by the Prosecution." There is considerable common sense in the arrangement. The consideration that the cross-examination by the Prosecution of the accused is part of an accused's case is not lost on an accused who still has a right of further cross-examination and to give evidence on his own behalf. The objection of the Defence to the second part of the motion is therefore refused. The Trial Chamber therefore rejects the motion for an order of appearance of the Defence witnesses, but grants the motion for the order of cross-examination. This is our ruling. We received an application for the Bajram holidays, which is indicated to be how many days between the 7th and 8th --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have submitted for 7 and 8 April, even though Bajram lasts for four days. However, I have only asked for the first two days and I think this is fully justified -- the two major Muslim holidays are the two Bajrams and I think that it falls well within the rights of both the accused and their Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Has the month of the Haj started -- I think it is starting today or tomorrow. Is it today or is it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is neither today nor tomorrow -- it is on 7 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what I asked you; has the month of the Haj started?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: In our calendar, it says that it is really the 7th and the 8th, and here in The Hague the Turkish community has also issued a calendar which starts on 7 April, and lasts for four days. I am not aware of any other dates and I think that this year this calendar is not controversial in any way. As far as I know, the Hajis have already embarked on their trip and, as far as I know, it is 7 and 8 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you not think the 7th alone should be sufficient, instead of stretching it too far? You can have the 7th. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I make several comments? Mr. Karabdic filed a request on behalf of all the accused and Defence counsel who celebrate this holiday, and I believe that it is reasonable that, out of four days, which constitute this holy festival, only two days are being requested, and I think that Mr. Karabdic has fully taken into account the wishes and feelings of all the accused and Defence counsel, as well as trying to balance it against the needs of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we also would like to know whether you can rule on it now so that we could proceed with making arrangements regarding the witness testimonies and order of witnesses and such, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose if you have both the 7th and the 8th, then you are expected to be here on the 9th. You will be here on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will have the 7th and the 8th and then you appear for your matters on 9 April. We should continue with the proceedings after lunch. Then we will hear what your opposition is, Mr.s Residovic. We will start at 2 o'clock. We will come back at 2 o'clock and continue with the Defence. (12.14pm).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We are back now and we will start with the Defence. Yes, Mr.s Residovic, I hear that you are starting with an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Before calling the first Defence witness, I should like to avail myself of the right, according to Rule 84 of the Rules of Procedure, to make a brief opening statement. Pursuant to Rule 84 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Defence counsel of Mr. Zejnil Delalic will begin with an opening statement in which we shall briefly indicate the method and aims of the presentation of evidence in this part of the criminal proceedings. Article 21 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal establishes the right of the accused to examine, or have examined, the witnesses against him under the same conditions as witnesses against him. This is Article 21(4)(e) of the Tribunal's Statute. Upon the completion of the part of the Prosecution case, the Defence counsel of Mr. Delalic has prepared evidence in Defence of the accused as the first among the four accused in this case. Evidence in favour of Mr. Zejnil Delalic's Defence begins precisely after Mr. Delalic has spent two years and 12 days in detention. Your Honours, this very fact is a clear indicator that Mr. Delalic has not been afforded the right to an expeditious trial. The rejection of his request for a separate trial, which is today already a Rule in proceedings in relation to other superior persons in cases before this Tribunal, Zejnil Delalic is in a position to participate in a trial which is far longer than would be necessary to establish his possible personal responsibility or to acquit him. There are other characteristics which we wish to draw the court's attention to with respect to Mr. Delalic. Only two persons have been arrested in accordance with Rule 40 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this Tribunal, that is, before an indictment was issued and confirmed against them -- Zejnil Delalic is one of those two persons. The arrest of Zejnil Delalic was carried out at the request of the Prosecutor, even though, as we have heard from the Prosecution witnesses during the time of arrest, there were no criminal charges made against him, nor was a warrant for his arrest issued by any country, nor by any domestic or international institutions. Zejnil Delalic was immediately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you please excuse me. I thought your opening speech relates to the evidence that you are leading in support of the case of the Defence. You do not go on to make comments or criticisms of matters which have already been done. What you are now to do is to tell the Trial Chamber the evidence you are leading. This is what an opening speech is made for. You should have had enough time to criticise the Prosecution's case and whatever has been time and you have sufficient time. You are still in charge of your case. Nothing stops you doing that subsequently. Outline before the Trial Chamber the evidence you are leading. If you do not think that is necessary, then call the accused person to give his evidence. It just does not make any sense going through what you might say later or subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is my intention to say how and why the Defence will present the evidence it intends to call, but the volume, quantity and quality of evidence is based on a prior period, which has put us in a certain position regarding the presentation of evidence. I have only two more facts to refer to regarding Mr. Delalic's position so far, and then I intend to go on to what we intend to present by way of evidence. I did not consider a short comment on the procedural position of my defendant would not be acceptable as the introduction to the presentation of its evidence. I therefore appeal to you to allow me to refer to these two additional facts and then to proceed as you have suggested. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may do so. I do not think it is really necessary as part of your case. This is what I am saying. It has nothing to do with your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As I just said, Zejnil Delalic was interrogated immediately after his arrest without the presence of an attorney, though it was assumed that the acts for which he was charged under Article 21 should entitle him to legal assistance -- in any case where the interests of justice so require, and this is a right that the accused could not waive. Availing himself of the right according to 89(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the trial has accepted much of the evidence requested by the Prosecutor and, finally, the Prosecutor submitted to the Defence on 25 March this year 11 documents indicating that it intends to use it as evidence, which means only five days before the beginning of the Defence case new evidence has been presented, which clearly shows that the Prosecutor is continuing the investigation, even after the completion of his case. All the above mentioned places the Defence of Mr. Delalic in a position that, even today, at the beginning of the presentation of the Defence case, it cannot determine completely neither the quantity of the evidence nor the time it will require to present it. The Defence of Mr. Delalic will present as much evidence as is necessary for Mr. Delalic to present a full Defence and to ensure a fair trial, fully convinced that this Trial Chamber will devote full attention to the right of the accused and ensure a fair trial as it is obliged to do under Article 20 of this Tribunal's Statute. Your Honours, the Defence will present evidence before this Trial Chamber which will show that Zejnil Delalic is innocent. The Prosecutor charges Zejnil Delalic of coordinating the activities of forces in the area of Konjic somewhere from April 1992 until September 1992, and that he was the commander of the first Tactical Group of the Bosnian forces, and that, in that period, and in those capacities, he was responsible for the work of a prison and held a position of superiority in relation to all guards in the camp and other individuals who entered the camp and mistreated the prisoners. Establishing the position of Zejnil Delalic as a person with superior responsibility over the prison, the Prosecution goes on to allege that Zejnil Delalic knew, or had reason to know, that his subordinates were committing criminal acts without taking the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts and punish the perpetrators. The Prosecutor cannot succeed, for the simple reason that Zejnil Delalic does not have the status of a superior. For these reasons, it is understandable that the Prosecutor should, in the opening statement, say that there was a great deal of discussion as to the authorisations Delalic had in paper in his opening statement. This is no wonder, because a coordinator is a new function that was established due to the complicated situation in Konjic at the time and there is no particular body that established competence over Celebici. Similarly, in his opening statement the Prosecutor alleged that others may share this competence, but that this cannot be a Defence for Zejnil Delalic. By this position, before presenting its own case, the Defence has a rather dangerous thesis before it for a criminal procedure. If we do not know who is responsible, then it is Zejnil Delalic. If we do not know which organ is responsible, then it is Zejnil Delalic. If others are responsible, then Zejnil Delalic is certainly as well. I am quite confident that this Trial Chamber will resolutely resist such an approach, and confirm here the supreme principle of any criminal proceedings in dubio pro reo, which means that in case of doubt, one must always take the side of the accused. The Defence will assist the Trial Chamber in establishing that Zejnil Delalic was never, in the time indicated in the indictment, responsible over the prison, nor its personnel. The Defence will present the following evidence before this Trial Chamber. First, it will invite and hear expert witnesses in the areas of history and military doctrine. It will call and hear witnesses who are familiar with the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Konjic. It will call and hear evidence who are familiar with the activities of Zejnil Delalic. It will tender a large number of documents for admission. It will show a number of videotapes and present other evidence in order to establish that Zejnil Delalic is not responsible for the charges brought against him. Though, in conformity with the Statute of the International Tribunal, individual responsibility is being tried, it is impossible to establish that individual responsibility without a broader understanding of the context of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Konjic itself, so that the Prosecutor, rightly, invited three expert witnesses, with the help of whom he tried to establish matters of significance for this case. The Prosecutor acted similarly in the Tadic case and other cases that are being tried before this Tribunal. In order to facilitate understanding of the overall situation and the actual events in Konjic in 1992, when allegedly the acts described in the indictment occurred, the Defence will call at least two expert witnesses -- Professor Iljas Hadzibegovic, an expert on the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Brigadier General Mohamed Vejzajic, a military expert, regarding the behaviour of the former JNA and the development of the BiH army after the proclamation of its independence. Both experts will present an overview of the general and military situation in Konjic in 1992 on the basis of their expertise and their own research on the ground. With the help of this and other evidence, the Defence will show that Bosnia and Herzegovina sought to establish its statehood over the centuries, that nurturing its way of life at a cross-roads between different civilisations Bosnia-Herzegovina has preserved its multi-ethnic, multi-religious and multi-cultural character as an essential characteristic, that it is impossible to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina according to ethnic criteria, without terrible violence; that the aspirations of neighbours to appropriate parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina or in its entirety have been present in history; that Bosnia and Herzegovina was attacked on the day that it proclaimed its independence; that the towns of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Konjic, were exposed to horrendous destruction and killing, that the legal organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina waged a battle and created their own army, that the legal authorities in Konjic invested a maximum of effort to avoid a conflict and, when the town was surrounded and attacked, they exerted maximum, one might say, superhuman efforts to ensure minimum conditions for the survival of the population, for the accommodation and nutrition and treatment of refugees from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to extend minimum medical assistance to numerous casualties and to ensure fairness, as much as possible, to people who were in detention. The evidence will show that the persons detained in Celebici were nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina, residents and, in most cases, of many years standing in Konjic, that at the time of the proclamation of an immediate threat of war they purchased and owned armaments, blocked roads, or participated in attacks against their own legal authorities, whereby there were reasonable grounds to suspect that they committed serious criminal offences under the criminal code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, that they were rebels; that criminal proceedings were instituted against at least 100 such persons; and that the persons detained in Celebici were not persons enjoying protection under the Geneva Conventions. With respect to Zejnil Delalic, the evidence which the Defence will present will show that as of April until at least 27 July he had absolutely no functions which would be a function of military or civilian superiority; namely, the evidence will show that Zejnil Delalic, until he took over the function of commander of Tactical Group number 1 after 27 July 1992, engaged only in logistical affairs and, as of 18 May 1992, he was also a coordinator as a predominantly civilian duty to which he was appointed by a civilian body, that is, the war presidency of the Konjic municipality. As a regular soldier, evidence will show that Zejnil Delalic spent the whole month of July 1992 in remote mountainous regions in combat activities without having any functions in the military sense and with a very concrete combat assignment. Throughout his stay in Konjic from April until the end of November 1992, the evidence will show that Zejnil Delalic was not a member of any political Party in Konjic and Bosnia-Herzegovina; that he was not elected or appointed to any State or any other body; that he was not a member of the war presidency, nor was he a member of bodies of political Parties or other institutions. The evidence will show that, in 1992, he was not a commander or a member of the municipal staff of Territorial Defence, which later became the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or a member of the joint command of the TO and the HVO in any period of time that year. The Defence evidence will also show that, after 27 July, Zejnil Delalic was appointed to a military function, that is, the commander of Tactical Group 1, with the military assignment to participate in lifting the blockade around Sarajevo under siege. In that capacity, he had forces and resources subordinated to him in the border area from Dreznica to Igman. However, the evidence of the Defence will show that, holding this military function, he did not have any superiority over the region, nor did he have any jurisdiction over the district staff or corps, nor did he have any jurisdiction over staffs and institutions in that area. All the evidence that the Defence will present before this Trial Chamber will show that Zejnil Delalic was at no time a person with superior command over the Celebici prison and its staff. Through the presentation of evidence we will also show the true Serbs who were subordinated to him while he was commander of Tactical Group 1 were not guards, nor Celebici prison staff, nor did any of his subordinate soldiers commit any of the alleged criminal offences according to the indictment. The evidence will also show that, as of April 1992, the defensive forces that were active in Konjic were the Territorial Defence, the Croatian Defence Council and the Ministry of the Interior, and that Zejnil Delalic never had a command position in relation to these bodies. We shall also show that the legal authorities from April 1992 organised the defence, and that there were no private armies or groups operating in this area. The Defence will establish all the above mentioned facts by calling witnesses, presenting documents, and showing videotapes of relevance in support of the Defence of the accused, Zejnil Delalic. In this stage, the Defence will not request protective measures for its witnesses, but if this should be in the interests of the protection of witnesses, such a request will be submitted to the Trial Chamber in due time. I do not wish to argue the particular points of the indictment, because Mr. Delalic's Defence already referred to those points in its motion for no case, and the same will be referred to during the presentation of evidence. Therefore, in concluding my opening statement, your Honours, the Defence will, availing itself of its rights under Article 21 and other provisions of the Statute, and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, present its evidence and thereby show that the accusations against Zejnil Delalic are unfounded. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you are leading evidence, not putting up arguments at this stage. You are entitled to lead whatever evidence you can in support of what subsequent arguments you want to put up. What else? Who is your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to call the first Defence witness, an expert witness in history. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I raise a matter at this stage, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, let us hear what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, last Thursday at 2.45pm the Defence served upon us all this material that your Honours see on the table here behind me -- an extensive amount of material which relates to the two expert witnesses that Madam Residovic has indicated she wishes to call, and, according to her order of list of witnesses, will be the next two witnesses in order. It has been impossible for the Prosecution to absorb all of this material. It is highly complex; there is large amounts of it which we will have to make decisions on in respect of whether or not it is material that we will object to or whether we consent to. There were three videotapes provided at 5pm on Friday by the Defence, for the first time. I have not seen them. As I understand, one of them could go for as long as two hours. One of them I have no idea what is contained in it -- I have not seen them, as I said. Your Honours, you will recall that we were in a similar position; we called two expert witnesses, and Mr. Ackerman addressed the court in relation to what he saw or said were our misdeeds concerning this issue of notice. In that case, what the Defence were complaining about was the fact that a CV had been given late, and a document had been given late, which was not intended to be tendered by the Prosecution and we never said it was intended to be tendered by the Prosecution, but it was merely made available for their assistance. Notwithstanding that, Mr. Ackerman said -- and I might just quote, because I think it is instrumentive to see what they said to us in situations which were far less grievous than what we are now confronting. He said: "I think it is a violation of all the obligations of the Prosecutor under the Rules of this court, and under the interpretation of those Rules by the court in the Blaskic case, to be providing us with us with this material in effect five minutes before the witness is to take the stand. This makes it absolutely impossible, and if not impossible certainly unlikely, that the Defence counsel have had any opportunity to prepare for a comprehensive and efficient cross-examination of this witness. I have no idea, and I will not suggest, that this was done intentionally by the Office of the Prosecutor so as to prevent us having information. I do not know this. But the Prosecutor's Office notified this court I think well over a month ago of their intentions to call this man." Your Honours, we have understood that this expert witness was going to be called by the Defence and they knew that they were going to call their expert witness much longer than a month ago. He goes on: "It is very difficult for me to accept that this material could not have been provided to us until five minutes before he is to take the stand. I think there is a number of remedies available to the court. One of those is to totally refuse to permit him to testify, because of the Prosecutor's violations of their obligations under the Rules, a second is to adjourn the court for a reasonable period of time to permit us to assimilate and explore the new information provided to us this morning. There is a wealth of information about this witness contained on the eight pages that we received." He is referring here to a CV. So, your Honours, in relation to a document that we had no intentions of tendering, and in relation to a curriculum vitae, Mr. Ackerman had that to say. As a consequence of that, your Honours gave the Defence relief in terms of the time that the Defence had to prepare for their cross-examination. We are in a much worse position. We are not dealing with the curriculum vitae, we are not dealing with a document which is merely background material -- we are dealing with material which, from the opening address, Madam Residovic has made clear she intends to tender. We are dealing with complicated issues, and we were given them in such an impossibly short period of time that there is no way that we could get ready, in that short time, to prepare an effective and efficient cross-examination. However, we are not seeking to delay these proceedings; we are not seeking to delay the calling of this witness. Our position is this: we submit that, if the Defence were entitled to an extensive period of time -- I can go into them, because your Honours know both Professor Economides, and Professor Gow, a considerable lapse of time passed between when they gave their evidence-in-chief and when they were ultimately finally cross-examined -- we are not asking the witness not be called, we are asking for the same indulgence in terms of the postponement of our cross-examination. We are not seeking anything extensive, we are merely asking that the cross-examination take place at the conclusion of the witnesses that have been arranged to testify this week, and no more and, in relation to the documents that are sought to be tendered, we ask that they do not seek to tender them until such time as the cross-examination is completed. We say that because we are hopeful that if we are given a sufficient period of time to examine these documents, that we can consent to some of them, and we can reduce the amount of time spent, which would otherwise be taken up in individually arguing and objecting to them as they arise. If we are given sufficient time, we believe that we can achieve this, which will be considerably more efficient from the point of view of court and far less tedious in terms of having to deal with them one document at a time. We will do everything in our best endeavours to accommodate the Defence in not objecting to documents if we can conceivably do so, in the interests of the Prosecution case, and in the interests of presenting before the court reliable and credible evidence. But, your Honours, we have been placed in this impossible position -- placed in it by the Defence -- and we are merely asking that we be extended the same considerations as were extended to them in a far less ingredious circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for giving us a forewarning of what you are likely to meet. Mr.s Residovic, what is your reply to this service on the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I reject all the objections made by the Prosecutor with respect to any failure to respect the obligations that the Defence has towards the Prosecution. According to the court's ruling, the Defence informed the Prosecution in time that it would call this witness and provide it with his CV. The Defence also informed the Prosecutor that it would be calling a military expert and, since that military expert was also a participant in the events, at their request we renounced calling this particular military expert. A month ago, we informed the Prosecution of the name of a new military expert, and thereby, respecting the ruling of this Trial Chamber, informed the Prosecution in a timely fashion regarding our expert witnesses. As for the right of the Prosecution to prepare for the cross-examination, I cannot speak about that at length, because both parties have the right to prepare for the cross-examination, but I would like to remind you, your Honours, that this case started on 10 March last year and the Prosecutor, which has at its disposal numerous institutions and resources, which is not the case with the Defence team, provided us with the expert finding of Professor Calic on 4 March, which means only six days prior to the beginning of the proceedings before this Trial Chamber. For this reason, I feel that the Defence has done nothing that would be in violation of the Rules of the Tribunal and that is why I reject such an objection. However, I do understand that the Prosecutor may need to review all the material and to prepare, but the Prosecutor is offering something that the Defence cannot accept and that is that, while examining this witness, we cannot tender documents for admission. In this way, we are placed in an unequal position regarding -- as compared to their own witness, Dr. Calic, who provided us, only six days before her appearance, extremely voluminous documentation and literature, which served as a basis for her testimony. Therefore, your Honours, if you accept the reasons presented by the Prosecutor that he needs time to prepare for the cross-examination, I propose that we postpone the testimony of our witnesses until the end of the week, that is, until the Prosecutor is ready to undertake the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think we have any intention of doing so. You may proceed with your witness and I think we will find a way of seeing when the cross-examination will take place. Just lead your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you call your first witness. Would you please have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, but could the usher please help me to have the witness brought in, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. ILJAS HADZIBEGOVIC Examined by MR.S RESIDOVIC

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your name for the Trial Chamber -- and state your full name and last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Iljas Hadzibegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 59 -- I will be 60 this year.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in a town called Bugojno, 135 kilometres south-west of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Can you tell us a few words about your profession -- can you tell us what you are by profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a historian by profession -- I work as a university professor.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: At what university do you teach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I work at the University of Sarajevo -- the School of Philosophy.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Where did you study, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed my studies at the Sarajevo University, and graduate studies I completed in Belgrade in 1967.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: What is the highest degree of education that you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received a Ph.D. in 1977, and in 1986 I became a full-time professor at the Sarajevo University.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, how many professors with the Ph.D. titles were at your school before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had 12 departments before the war in our school and we had about 150 Ph.D.s -- professors.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell me how many professors are there left today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 50 and 60.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, when did you defend your thesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in 1977.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: What was your doctoral thesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My doctoral thesis was the emergence of the working class in Bosnia and its history until 1914. This was a thesis covering both the social and economic history.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Since when have you been with the University of Sarajevo, School of History?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first worked as an assistant at the historical institute for five years between 1964 -- starting in 1964, and starting on 1 January 1970 I moved to the School of Philosophy and that is where I have been since. I became a docent in 1978 and, after three years, I was elected an associate professor and since 1986 I am a full-time professor and that is the capacity now in which I work to date.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, in this period, you probably conducted research work. Can you tell us, where did you do your research -- at what universities and at what institutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have a tradition, to research the archives that are the closest to us, and that was among the Yugoslavs, it is the Sarajevo one which has about 20 million documents and then Belgrade -- Zagreb, Dubrovnik and so on. Since Bosnia was for about 40 years under the Austro-Hungarian rule, I spent time researching in Vienna, and the archives in Vienna, the National Library for (INAUDIBLE) Archive and other libraries are very important for all of the Balkan history. I also did some research briefly in Budapest in the Hungarian State archive and in the National Library in Budapest. I also did some research in Prague and I also had an opportunity to spend an extended period of time in Munich in the Institute for South Eastern European Studies, as well as in Vienna, where I was, for a while, I was invited to work as an expert -- I had a grant to do study on a population which unfortunately I have not yet completed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you, professor. Is it true that you have published about 100 articles from the area of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is true that I have published around that number of units and I have not counted in all the articles and studies that have not yet been published.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, what is your narrower area of interest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the -- my narrow expertise is the history of Bosnian people in the late 19th and 20th century as well as the south Slav people of that same period.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Is it true that you have published two books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I first published in 1980 the book that bore the title of my doctoral thesis and my second book was published in 1991, "The towns of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the late 19th and early 20th century", which was an attempt to study the dynamics between the tradition and modern development in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Is it true that you are the author and co-author of numerous publications which have been provided as an annex to your expert report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have only given select bibliography in the annex of my expert report and I believe that this is proper information given that -- the nature of the report. I have -- the major topics that I have included were the political movements and social movements in Bosnia-Herzegovina. More recently, I have researched migration and its impact on the ethnic relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is very closely related to the most recent events in both Bosnia-Herzegovina and the ex-Yugoslavia territory.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, could you please tell the Trial Chamber when did you publish your first expert work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I published it in 1962 while I was still a student.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And when did you publish your last work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My last work was published early this year and its title was, "Civic Society in Bosnia-Herzegovina: its Origins and its Historical Context."

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, is it correct that your research directly relates to the history of the former Yugoslavia as well as the contemporary history of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, would you please tell me where did you spend the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 to 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 1992 and mid August 1994, I was in the besieged Sarajevo. After that, I left due to family and health circumstances and I went to Vienna. I worked there for a while, while my family stayed in Munich.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, can you confirm to this Trial Chamber that, as an eminent expert and scholar from Bosnia-Herzegovina, you are able to objectively view the events that you have been involved in and that you can provide a balanced judgement on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I am a historian by profession and the historian that does not respect the truth cannot work as a historian.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: In compiling this report, can you tell us what sources you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When compiling this report, I first -- I used my own work, then the work of a number of experts in this field, that is, the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 19th and 20th century. I also used the relevant material which is archived at the institute for the research into war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which provided precious material to me. Also, the statistical institute provided me very valuable material and from them I received very valuable statistical information. I have also used material that has been published in Sarajevo in this period, and in the Sarajevo media, as well as media elsewhere. I also used video material that was provided to me through the TV Sarajevo as well as the TV in Konjic and Srebrenica. I also used material that was provided by my colleagues, Docent Marie-Janine Calic and Dr. Gow. I also used documents that were provided to me by the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, through your -- did you try to verify certain documents that you received from various sources through your own research?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Verification of documents is a continuing process -- it is an activity that has to go on and until each document's authenticity has been fully confirmed, this is an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, finally, can you tell me, do you base your report and your testimony today on the facts that have been adequately verified and confirmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that -- I have based my report on trustworthy facts, because there were many facts -- there were many documents which I have not included, because I did not feel that they were adequately verified. However, everything that I have included, I have put into this report, I believe that, at least at this stage of the research process, I think that they have been adequately confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: On the basis of this answer, can you tell me, did you encounter any difficulties during your efforts to draft this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. This is something that any historian finds himself fighting against in a situation when you have contemporary events. Many events have not been fully developed or completed, because we had a war some documents are missing. However, over a period of time and despite all the difficulties, I think that we can compile adequate and valuable facts. I believe that of course, in time, certain conclusions will be further confirmed in details.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, were you approached by the Defence for Mr. Zejnil Delalic at some point last year and asked to appear here as an expert witness in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Defence did approach me to appear here as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Obviously, you accepted to come here since you are here today. Can you now please tell us how long a time did you spend preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I was first approached about a year ago, but I think that I have spent the last six months fully involved in the project, whereas the first six months was probably less intensive.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, I would now like to ask you to identify what it was that you worked on the last six months and that we have provided to the Defence and what we are offering to the Trial Chamber today. So, I would like to ask you, professor, is it true that you compiled an expert report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to offer this report for identification and show it to the witness. The Defence has provided enough copies for the Trial Chamber. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I assume it is only being marked for identification at this stage, your Honour -- yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document 135/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would like to indicate we will have an objection to the tendering of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is this the report that you compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the report that I have compiled.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender the expert's report by Dr. Iljas Hadzibegovic into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object to the tendering of the report. The basis of my objection is, firstly, that the witness is here to testify and seemingly what is sought to be done by the Defence is to not only proceed with the witness through evidence-in-chief by way of oral testimony, but to cover the same ground in the form of a statement, which, in my submission, your Honours, is an inappropriate way to proceed. The best evidence that your Honour can receive is what the witness says. There are numerous issues and points of objection that are contained in this report, which the Prosecution would have to then deal with individually before it could in any way agree to its admission, whereas these matters are much better and effectively dealt with by the witness being taken through the evidence in the usual fashion, and asked the questions and then, should matters arise at that stage, the Prosecution can take its objection, if necessary. But just to simply, through the back-door, try and put this report in, simply on the basis that it is identified as an expert report, in our submission, is objectionable. Furthermore, the report itself is based on the large volumes of documents that we were given so belatedly last week, to which there are numerous objections that we, at this stage, would wish to make, because we have not had anywhere near a sufficient amount of time to finally decide whether or not we can agree to their admission. As such, our position is at the moment we have to indicate that we find the exhibits objectionable. So, the report itself makes reference and purports to rely upon the very material that we seek to object to. Your Honours, on that ground, it is the equivalent of calling a witness and endeavouring to tender a statement at the same time. We find that process objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I really do not appreciate this objection. Are you doubting whether he prepared it, or the basis under which he did it, or its usefulness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The basis of the objection is that it contains material that we would wish to take objection to and that the witness is here and that the usual and ordinary course is for this witness or for any witness, whether it be an expert or an ordinary fact witness, to be taken through the evidence. One does not call a witness, tender their statement, and then seek to examine them. That is not the appropriate course to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I will admit it for identification at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can carry on with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I proceed, your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I proceed, your Honour -- yes. Mr. Professor, did you prepare this report on the basis of documents contained in this folder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask this folder, on the basis of which this report was compiled, to be identified. We have sufficient copies for your Honours. Then we can see whether the witness recognises the documents on the basis of which he compiled his report and prepared for testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure it is being disputed that he prepared the report which is admitted for identification. Nobody is disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I appreciate sincerely the experience of this Trial Chamber and of the Prosecutor. I am following the same procedure that the Prosecutor applied when calling Dr. Calic. I have no other experiences with this Tribunal, and I think I am acting correctly and in order with the procedure determined for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document D136/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, will you please look at the table of contents of this folder that you have on the table? Is it the folder containing materials which you used in preparation for this testimony and for your report? Are you having problems with the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am hearing the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, will you please open this binder and tell me whether these are the documents that you based your expert opinion on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Are these the documents that you worked with when drawing up your report and your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could these documents be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object to the documents being admitted into evidence, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why you objecting to it? They are not documents on which he relied for his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am not basing my objection on that. I am basing my objection on numerous of the documents that are contained in here (a) because we do not know the source of them so therefore are in no position to make any assessment as to their reliability; (b) some of the documents are in the form of statements or ways of avoiding statements, because they are letters written to Madam Residovic saying, "I am informing you the following things have taken place," or, "the following position is correct." Under no basis could I see that as admissible. There are some documents which presumably, if we understood the relevance of them, then we may not have any objection to them at all. What is sought to be done here, your Honours, is that there is a process going on that the statement and a huge binder of documents, are sort to be just thrown in and we are sitting here try to say whether we are object to some and not the others. We are not given the opportunity -- it is goes in as one blanket document. If they are marked for identification, that is a different matter because we can deal with them in the appropriate way. If they are sought to be tendered, we object to them being tendered in this way. We have indicated we have not had an opportunity to fully assess them and make a final determination. We must object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it your argument that you can object to a document that somebody relies upon for his opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not seeking to object to it on that basis. If it is sought to be tendered as to the truth of the contents, then I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think they are saying that is the truth of what is being tendered. They are merely saying they are the documents on which he relied for what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If they are not sought to be tendered as to the truth of the contents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is a report. He has indicated the sources upon which he has based his report. There are so many statements in this document. You can question him with regard to the source upon which he has based that opinion. It is merely his opinion. He was not present there personally. This is a report. You can cross-examine him with reference to the document which is the basis of a particular statement in this report. He has given a list of all these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is depriving me of the right to object to the documents being tendered into evidence -- the very thing the Defence spent many, many hours doing. The documents seized in Vienna were objected to. I had to go through individually and establish the relevance and admissibility of each one. The Defence come here and hand up a huge binder of documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They are not saying those are documents which he now uses -- they are documents on which he relied. It does not mean those documents are correct. It does not tell you that they have been authenticated by anybody. It is documents he relied on. That is a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My objection falls away to some extent so long as there is no attempt whatsoever for the Defence to rely on them for the truth of their contents. If the Defence are trying to rely on them for the truth of their contents, then I have to object at this stage, because it is too late after they are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They could not have relied on them as the truth of what they contain -- that is a different matter. He relied on them for what he was saying. It does not necessarily mean that those things are correct. Somebody else might draw a different conclusion from what he has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: One wonders why it is necessary to tender them. They could be marked for identification for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: On the same basis as the report which he has produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam Residovic said she was tendering them. If they are only going to be marked for identification, I am sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They cannot be superior to what he has produced from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, professor, to look at these maps first and then to tell us whether these maps were used by you as a basis for compiling your expert opinion and report. We have a sufficient number of maps for the Trial Chamber and the witness. Could they be marked for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document D 137/1. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
