utterances.text: Professor, I shall now, after the identification, show you three videotapes and I am asking you to tell me whether these tapes, too, were used by you as a basis for compiling your report and in the preparation for your testimony here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence exhibit number 138/1, 139/1, and 140/1. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those, Sir, are they the videotapes that you used in compiling your expert report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these are the tapes that I used when preparing my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could they be marked for identification and admitted as the basis on which the expert witness compiled his expert report and which serves as a basis for his testimony before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They have been admitted for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I shall try to clarify through your testimony the historical, political and other events that occurred in the territory of the former Yugoslavia after 1980 and in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the town of Konjic after 1990. However, in view of your expert finding and in view of the fact that we all understand that current events do not occur in an historical vacuum, I will also put to you some questions from the more distant past. I am familiar with the historical principle that the present is the daughter of the past and the mother of the future, and that, without an understanding of some more distant events which decisively affected the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as events in the recent past, it is not possible to understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object. We either ask questions or we do not. This is nothing more than just a speech and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly put your question to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, will you please tell us briefly when Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed as a State and what happened in that first initial period in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina is mentioned for the first time in the middle of the 10th century in the work of the Byzantine King in 904, Constantine. It is mentioned on a small area of a small area of the banks of a river of the same name as an area which changed hands from the weaker to the more powerful neighbours.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, to be able to be as brief as possible, would you put on the ELMO map number M1, and indicate very briefly the main points of that historical period that are related to the current events or the latest events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have before us a map of the medieval Bosnian State. This is a map of the medieval Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, the changes that occurred from the 10th century, because the area marked in red is the area called Horjon Bosnijonen mentioned by King Constantine in the 10th century. This large area in pink is Bosnia in the 12th century, and the line in dark red is indicative of Bosnia at the peak of its power when it became a kingdom and this was in 1377, and this line in dark green indicates the borders of present day Bosnia-Herzegovina (indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us where Bosnia-Herzegovina is situated -- did its position affect its present-day history?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina is a land whose geographic and historical position was determined by history, because it was situated at the cross-roads of a number of civilisations -- originally, it was at the division between the eastern and western empire, that is, the division between Catholicism and Orthodoxy. Then, again, it found itself on the border between the Ottoman empire and the Habsburg empire, one bringing Islam and the other Catholicism. In modern history, again, a third line of division crossed Bosnia and the Yugoslav lands, and that was that it was between the eastern and western block and that it was always between two worlds -- the eastern part of it being inclined towards Orthodoxy and Islam and the western towards Catholicism. In more modern history and the political divisions that occurred, the eastern and western block met in Yugoslavia and therefore in Bosnia-Herzegovina this coincides with the present situation, because again the eastern and western part of Yugoslavia was divided, in this sense in terms of religion, civilisation and culture.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us rise. We will come back at 4 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can we have the witness brought back in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr.s Residovic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, I would like to apologise to both you and the Trial Chamber that I forgot to forewarn you. We both speak the same language. However, all that we are saying needs to be heard by the Trial Chamber, so we need to allow the interpreters to convey it to them. So, I would like to ask you now -- you see a set of headsets on your desk -- will you please listen in just for the sound of it and, when that is done, then please proceed with your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell us briefly what are the main characteristics of the relations between the different religious groups during the Ottoman period, which continued to date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina during the middle ages was a multi-religious and multi-ethnic province. This multi-ethnic feature continued after the fall of the medieval Bosnian State in 1453. After the Turkish take-over, the history of Islam ensues in addition to the Orthodox and Catholic religions and this produces the population of today, known as Bosniaks. At the end of the 15th century, a fourth religion is added -- the Jews from Spain resettled in Sarajevo and that is where they stay to date. This mosaic continues in Bosnia for 415 years and, later on, it would expand during the Austro-Hungarian period.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: When the Ottoman empire withdrew from the Balkans, did this have significant consequences to the local population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The withdrawal of the Ottoman empire lasted for almost two centuries, and it also implied withdrawal of the Muslim population, predominantly the Turkish population and out of Europe through the Bosphorous and into Anatolia. My apologies, this withdrawal was caused by one -- to transfer the population from the lost territories and in the other case, it was the annihilation of all the heritage -- this is the case in Greece, in Vlaska, Moldavia and later on in Serbia and still later in Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the Austro-Hungarian monarchy? I would like to especially draw our attention to the creation of the constitution for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia came under the Austrian rule in 1878 and its status was -- in fact, it was Austria that received the mandate from the European powers through the Berlin Congress, and the relationship between Austria and Hungary was set out in a separate contract and Bosnia was annexed to the Austro-Hungarian empire in 1908 and it received a separate constitution and its first provision was that it was a corpus separatum, it did not belong to Austria or Hungary so it was a corpus separatum, and the Bosnian becomes part of political life of that empire. It has no legislative powers but it could cooperate with the legislative bodies in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, did Bosnia-Herzegovina during the Austro-Hungarian rule as a corpus separatum, did it cover predominantly the current borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the Berlin Congress, Bosnia-Herzegovina had 51,027 square kilometres and these are the borders that Bosnia had when it entered Yugoslavia in 1918.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: The State constitution which you just mentioned, is a copy of this constitution included in this report as annex A1? (Handed). Could we just take a look at a copy of this State constitution and I think that you have already explained what it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we also have a translation -- an English translation --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Yes, this is part of the file that you have provided. Professor, how was Bosnia included into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes after the breakdown of Austria-Hungary after World War I and what was its status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first Yugoslavia State, or the Kingdom of Serb, Croats and Slovenes, was formed on 1918, on 1 December. Bosnia-Herzegovina became part of that State together with the lands that were under Austria-Hungary, including Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. They formed a single entity and they united with the Kingdom of Serbia, which also included Montenegro and Vojvodina and on 1 December they all united and, within its territorial borders, which were guaranteed by the first constitution of 1920, provision 135, guaranteeing its borders under the Austro-Hungarian rule, and it was not established -- constituted as a separate unit.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, the article 135 of the constitution of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes that you just quoted, is this the document which was marked as annex A2 in your folder -- your supporting folder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, can you tell me, what was the territorial and administrative division in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the period of Kingdom of Yugoslavia; that is, what were the reasons for such divisions, if they took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most significant division in Yugoslavia was introduced by the dictatorship of 6 January 1929, when the dynasty, that is, the court and the Serbian oligarchy attempted to create a unitarian State to obliterate the historical borders and, at that time, the State was divided into nine Banovinas, and the historical names were not respected, but the Banovinas drew their names from the names of rivers -- all provinces bore the names of different rivers, and Bosnia was split into four different Banovinas whereby its century-long tradition -- both the tradition as a State and as of its autonomy was thereby annihilated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the technical booth to display the map, page 1/3. I would like you then to elucidate the points you have just made to us when this map is displayed. Could you please just wait until the map is displayed on the ELMO. What does this map represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the map of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia of 1929 in which you can see nine Banovinas and the district of Belgrade. I would please like to ask to have the current borders of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina to overlap this over the map that is displayed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Can we please have the technical booth do that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In red line are indicated the borders of the present-day Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is the territory which we saw in the previous map of 1918, and the current one. We can see that Bosnia was divided between Drinska, Vrbaska, Primorska and Zetska Banovinas, so we can see that part had been annexed to Serbia and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, why is the agreement Cvetkovic-Macek often mentioned during the analysis of this period? Could you please explain to us the map marked as 1/4, and I would like the technical booth please to display this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have according to the Banovinas and the larger map is the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement-based map of Bosnia, which was signed 26 August 1939 and that means four days before the beginning of World War II. What this map reflects is the fact that the unitarian concept of Yugoslavia did not work and that Serbs and Croats proceeded to adopt an agreement. They wanted to create a Yugoslavia with three units -- one would be Slovenia, one Croatian Banovina and one the Serbian lands.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Based on map H 1/4/1, would you comment on the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina according to this division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see that Bosnia-Herzegovina was partly in the Posavina region, the three counties have been annexed to the Croatian Banovina and in the south-western part of Bosnia, several additional counties were annexed to the Croatian Banovina. The remaining territory was supposed to be part of the Serbian lands. This was a compromise between the Serbian and Croatian national movement leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your report, and this is a frequent case in the scholarly analysis, you mentioned the project of Greater Serbia. Can you please explain what this concept means and what is particularly -- in particular, what it means for Bosnia-Herzegovina. In order to facilitate that, could the technical booth please display the map H1/5? Also, could the technical booth display H1/5/1 right away so that we can see how Bosnia-Herzegovina looks there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr.s Residovic, I am not sure what you intend to show by this. What do you want to flesh out? It is an interesting historical discussion -- I do not deny that. What, in terms of your case, do you think this is intended to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the beginning, I said that we called an expert witness, a historian, to give us a very brief summary of a thousand years of history, which were some of the root causes for the conflict which took place in the early 90s, with a breakdown of Yugoslavia, and since my client has been associated with the activities of the Bosnian forces during the events, and I believe that we have covered 900 years very fast -- I think that we are arriving at 1990s any moment -- I think that it would be helpful if we provided a full context and covered the historical facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not saying anything about your style or what you intend to do. My apprehension is what all this meant. You understand what your case is and what you expect it to do? I do not see the relevance. That is speaking for myself. I am not talking about my colleagues. They might have their own attitude towards proving what you are asserting. A lot of the historical incidents are not in dispute -- nobody is denying that. If there is any dispute at all, it might relate to the current areas -- not the history before this time. It is your case. I have always preferred a tidier and more expeditious way of getting at where we are going.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is my endeavour, too. I think that the witness's testimony will focus on Konjic, but you will recall about the TO and HVO, the Republika Srpska. In order to understand all these categories in case, it is not so easy -- maybe even for us who have lived through this period. I think that it will assist you when you make final determinations if you are able to get the full context of all the events that took place there. I am really trying to be brief. I will do my utmost to get there fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am trying to avoid being not confused by too much detail -- this is my problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you said that this was a project known as Greater Serbia. Does it include parts of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of it, except the part that was attached to Croatia in the south-west and in the north, in the Sava River valley. The rest of Bosnia was attached to Serbia, or rather to the Serb lands, as they were known.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The concept of a Greater Croatia is also customary in your historical and scholarly reviews. Could you tell us, please, on the map, H1/6 -- could you show us what that idea means for Bosnia-Herzegovina? Could the technicians show us H1/6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map shows in yellow the area of the independent State of Croatia established on 10 April 1941 as a puppet State created by fascist Germany and Fascist Italy.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Would you please show over this map the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- H1/6/1, and will you please tell us how the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina was affected by this project?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we see that the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was included in the independent State of Croatia. This marked the fulfilment of the concept of a Greater Croatia and, when a debate is going on between Yugoslav and world historians as to the borders between Serbia and Croatia, the Serbian extremists wished to attach Bosnia to Serbia, then the border is on the Una River. When on the other hand a Greater Croatia thesis is advocated, then the boarder is on the Drina River, so that these two interests collided throughout history at the expense of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this can be seen also on this map, because, in its entirety, it was included in that State. May I add in this connection that all these changes were accompanied by extreme suffering of the population, both Serbs, Croats and Muslim populations, and, during the Second World War, ethnic cleansing was already introduced in programmes and in practice. Hence, we feel it is necessary to draw attention to the roots of the evil, which was repeated in the 20th century and Bosnia-Herzegovina was rebuilt three times from the ashes, with vast human and material destruction and that is why we think it is not -- it would be a good idea to try and find some solution so that such things should not be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this radical Ustasha concept has, on the other extreme, the Chetnik concept of a Greater Serbia, so would you please explain to us that concept on map H1/7? Can I ask the technicians to show us number 7 and, again, H1/7/1, could you overlay Bosnia-Herzegovina on top of this map so that we see how it is affected by this project?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of Yugoslavia -- the area in white shows that the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina is included in Greater Serbia -- actually, in Serbia -- which was designed in such a way that it came to life in this war. The idea was that it would stretch to Karlobag in the north and include all these territories not only in Bosnia-Herzegovina but also in Croatia where the Serb population was residing so that is the root of the idea of all Serbs in one State, and this corresponds to present-day history.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, briefly what the programme of the Chetnik movement was, because their Honours were listening to some witnesses and wanted this concept to be clarified for their benefit. You have discussed this in your documents and in annex number 6, in particular. Annex A6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you have the most important abstract from the Chetnik programme translated into English. The author of this programme was Draza Mihajlovic, who was a colonel of the Yugoslavia army, and commander of the Chetnik army in the country. He was, for a time, also Minister of the King in exile -- a Minister in the Government in exile.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, does that programme imply the disappearance of the Muslim population from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is reference here to the creation of Serb territories and these are listed. It is stated that they have to be ethnically pure and it is also envisaged that the non-Serb population should be removed. There are all kinds of possibilities envisaged, from killings to persecution and banishment and expulsions, so that this programme actually served as a basis in this war, too.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell me, in view of the fact that these two projects, the Chetnik and the Ustasha, came to expression in the Second World War, what was the attitude of the Muslim population and their intellectuals towards the crimes committed against the Serbs, the Jews and other peoples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to show, through the resolutions passed by the Muslim people in the most important towns in 1941, whereby it denounced the crimes committed against the Serb people, and it also disassociates itself from the Muslims in the Ustasha movement who participated in the commission of those crimes. Therefore, this is something that was set in motion by Muslim priests in Sarajevo and then such resolutions were passed in Sarajevo, Mostar, Zenica, Bijeljina and other towns. This was one of the rare anti-fascist moves taken against fascism in those days in Europe.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: What is the importance for the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the anti-fascist struggle of the peoples of Yugoslavia and of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of the Second World War, three ideas came together -- one was the greater Croatian idea; the second the greater Serbian; and the third idea was the anti-fascist national liberation idea which sought to unite the peoples of Yugoslavia and of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It emerged victorious in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, could we now see map H8/1 for you to explain to us what that meant as a result of the anti-fascist struggle of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of Yugoslavia created in the course of the Second World War and, finally, regulated as a State -- a Federal State with six equal republics -- not only were they equal -- not only were the republics equal but so were the Yugoslavia peoples. All the republics had certain ethnic characteristics, whereas Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a multi-ethnic State, also acquired a -- it was also an independent republic on a completely equal footing with the other Yugoslavia republics. This is a map that remained in force until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with this we come to the end of the brief review of the history of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the peoples living in it and we would now like to ask the professor to move on to latter-day history, which we have asked you to testify about before this Trial Chamber. Will you please, professor, explain to us the main characteristics of the crisis in the former Yugoslavia after 1980, that is, after the death of the President of SFRY, that is Josip Broz Tito. So as not to go into excessive details, will you please tell me first whether the crisis was first initially an economic or political crisis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The death of Josip Broz Tito, the President of the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia at the time speeded up the crisis and the destruction of the Yugoslavia society. It started as an economic crisis, which was particularly expressed in the form of very high external debts of Yugoslavia, which amounted to $US22 billion, and even though attempts were made through a crisis commission, and long-term programmes of economic stabilisation, the crisis was too deep and it could not be overcome, so that it soon developed into a social and political crisis. The ideology of Communism was called in question and solutions had to be sought in the form of new ideas.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, were there differences in terms of ways of dealing with the crisis among the individual Yugoslavia republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course there were differences and they were not only due to that crisis, but to previous history due to which there were different outlooks regarding social development. In the first place, Slovenia and Croatia wanted to develop a democratic society with a market economy, with more democracy, and with the ultimate goal of forming national States, whereas Serbia and Montenegro wanted to create a State which would be a centralised State and which would be controlled from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, under those circumstances, what did the Memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences issued in 1986 mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences was actually an analysis made by prominent intellectuals, members of the Serbian Academy headed by Antonije Isakovic. That document said that Serbia was a loser since the 1974 constitution, because, as opposed to the period before that, in 1974, it became only one of six equal republics. As a way out of the crisis, the intellectuals proposed three stages -- in the first stage, Serbia proper should strengthen its authority; then the second stage would consist of a centralisation in Serbia; and the third stage would be the creation of a Greater Serbia. In the first stage, Slobodan Milosevic and people who thought like him first tried and succeeded -- I beg your pardon -- something first had to be done to achieve greater homogeneity and to do that Milosevic went through various institutions -- first of all he cleansed the media from disobedient editors. Then he carried out changes in the Party leaderships, that is, removing the moderates and then, when he gained control of the media and strengthened his position in the Party, he then sought and dealt with the problem of disobedience. Then came the second stage -- the stage of centralisation of Serbia. This meant abolishing the autonomies of the two autonomous provinces, i.e. Vojvodina and Kosovo. It also involved changing the leadership in Montenegro so as to form a territory for Serbia, which would serve as a basis for further expansion and for control over Serbian lands outside the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro. Through the media, of which he already had control, and which were run by his followers, public rallies were organised, massive rallies in cities, and the moderate leaderships were removed and in their place Slobodan Milosevic's followers were appointed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: To speed up things, did the forces in Serbia succeed in their centralisation efforts and in abolishing the autonomies of Kosovo and Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a parallel process going on. The strongest resistance was put up by the Albanians who did not wish to give up their autonomy. They had 90 per cent of the population in Kosovo which was Albanian. They had their formed national institutions and they did not wish to give up that autonomy. There were fierce clashes between the army and the police, which sought to stifle the demonstrations in Kosovo. As a result of all these clashes was the failure of the Albanians to retain their autonomy, the constitution was amended and, on 28 March 1989, Serbia acquired a new constitution, a centralised Serbia. Slobodan Milosevic was elected President of Serbia and, in Novi Sad, Podgorica and Pristina, the leaderships were loyal to Slobodan Milosevic. That was the upshot of the memorandum, as well as of the other political tendencies that were in evidence in the country at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, after 1990, and the democratic elections in Slovenia and Croatia, new democratic forces appeared on the political stage. How did Belgrade react to those changes and what is the substance of the proclaimed slogan in Belgrade, "All Serbs in one country"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After these changes, it became clear, and especially after the failed 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, which was interrupted and then resumed -- at that Congress, the League of Communists made a statement that it no longer wanted to have a monopoly over political power in the country. This was followed by a process, during which the League of Communists disappeared from the historical scene, as did the single-Party system. This meant that processes were set in motion, the aim of which was to establish a balance between various political concepts. The concepts advocated by Slovenia and Croatia, which wanted to develop democratic societies and to form their own national States, and another concept advocated by Serbia and Montenegro and that was to preserve Yugoslavia, which would have a centralised federation, the centre being in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, the question that I put to you regarding the slogan, "All Serbs in one State", was it a call for changing the boundaries of the existing Yugoslavia republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Milosevic said at the time that he would not recognise republican boundaries if Yugoslavia fell apart. This meant that he would create a State following ethnic lines rather than historical boundaries. Therein lay the basis of the idea of all Serbs in one State. This, after all, was drawn into the plan called "framework", which covered the whole of Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and parts of Croatia in which the majority of the population were Serbs. This was a situation in which, when all this existed and had been plotted, efforts were made to achieve greater homogeneity of Serbs in other territories, and the Serbian national movement in Croatia became more radical, with the assistance and protection of the Yugoslavia People's Army, which increasingly acquired the characteristics of a Serbian army. In 1990, 60 per cent of the armed forces were Serbs -- even though Serbia constituted a far smaller proportion of the population.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, so as to avoid going into the war in Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia, I should like to ask you to tell us, after the withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of the Republic of Slovenia and Croatia, where was the majority of the forces of the former JNA deployed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of those forces were withdrawn to Bosnia-Herzegovina. All the forces that had withdrawn from Slovenia and from Croatia were deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- even three additional corps were brought in from Montenegro, Serbia and Vojvodina, the Novi Sad, Uzice and Podgorica Corps, so that Bosnia was overpopulated by the army, and this actually constituted what some people called "a quiet occupation", but in fact it was covering the entire territory and establishing full control over all resources, all communication lines, within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your brief review of the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you ascertained that, throughout this long period in history, it was a multi-ethnic State. Could I please ask you to look at map H1/9 and 9/1, and to show us what the actual ethnic situation was in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war broke out in 1992, so could the technicians please show us these maps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an ethnic map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, based on the 1991 population census. We see the ethnic composition of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the blue indicating Muslims/Bosniaks; the brown are Croats; the yellow are Serbs; and the pale blue, the others. So, this map shows that, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was not a single municipality -- and there were 109 of them-- that were ethnically 100 per cent pure.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, you have just told us that each of these circles represents one municipality, reflecting the colours of the three dominant peoples. Were they the only peoples living in 1992 just before the outbreak of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not the only peoples, because, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to the 1991 census, there were about 70 different statements regarding ethnic origin, but, in realistic terms, in addition to Serbs, Croats and Muslims, there were another 20 ethnic groups residing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, this was really a multi-ethnic community -- multi-ethnicity was a permanent characteristic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the middle ages to the present day.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: What was the result of the elections that were held in 1990 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and which political Parties won most seats in the Bosnian assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the elections held in November 1990, the national Parties were victorious -- the Party of Democratic Action, the Muslim Bosniak Party won the most votes. In a Parliament with 240 deputy seats, it won 86, or 35.83 per cent. The Serbian Social Democratic Party won 72 seats, or 30 per cent of the total number of seats in Parliament. The Croatian Democratic Alliance won 44 seats, or 17.33 per cent, I think. So that the national Parties won an absolute majority of seats, that is, 202 out of a total of 240. All the remaining Parties won a total of 38 seats, or -- I cannot remember what that was percentage wise.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, since the period that you are talking about right now is the period of the dissolution of Yugoslavia, could you tell us whether Bosnia-Herzegovina, as one of the Federal units within Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its political leadership, had a significant influence on the dissolution of Yugoslavia and can you tell us what was the thrust of the resolution proposed by President Izetbegovic and Gligorov and which you used in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already stated the differences which existed between different republics within Yugoslavia, that the concepts of Slovenia and Croatia were different than the positions of Serbia and Montenegro. The two weakest republics, that is Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia, were attempting at that time to do something in order to avoid the war. The Presidents of republics and autonomous provinces met six times in order to try to resolve this constitutional crisis. The last attempt was made by the Presidents Gligorov and Izetbegovic -- they attempted to find a compromise between the two concepts. They proposed to preserve an alliance of States or republics -- that is, a Yugoslavia identity be preserved. Slovenia and Croatia adopted decisions to proclaim their independence and to create national States.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Did this position yield any results?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This platform did not yield any results, and peace could not be preserved.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, the things that you just stated, is this platform part of your supporting material as annex D1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, let me take you back to certain issues regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina of this period. Can you tell me what was the position with respect to the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the three main political Parties? That is, the Serbian SDS, the Bosniak SDA and the Croat HDZ Parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The national parties cooperated in questions of winning the elections and removing the communists from power. Following that, their positions followed their own courses. They did not have the same positions with respect to the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: The Social Democratic Party -- you mean the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am sorry, I mean the Party of Democratic Action, and the Croatian Democratic Union, from the very beginning, cooperated very closely, and they wanted a sovereign and independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, while the SDS advocated for Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, what are the key elements or factors in the establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign independent State towards the end of 1991 and in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several factors which contributed to the establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent State. First of all, it is a long historical period -- a long period of history -- of its identity as a State and its long survival within the borders of the Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian empires. Another factor which is also very significant is the referendum through which the majority of the population elected for Bosnia-Herzegovina to become independent, and the third would be its struggle to preserve the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This would be some of the main elements that contributed to the establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent State. One of the key factors is obviously the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the European Union and other nations and its acceptance by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: What was the role of the former JNA in the dissolution of Yugoslavia and the war that ensued and I would like you to be very brief there and illuminate it for me, the historical rather than the military perspective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA, first of all -- in fact, it was permeated by nationalism -- not just Yugoslavia People's Army but also the Yugoslavia political leadership, so the JNA started arming and protecting only one segment of the population by becoming a single ethnic group-based army -- it lost its Yugoslavia character. It protected one ethnic group only, and therefore stopped being the factor which used to be the guarantee of the constitutional arrangements in Yugoslavia. It protected the Serbs in Croatia and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It armed them and it prepared them for a creation of a Greater Serbia -- to put it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Professor, you said that SDS was one of the victors of the election in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990 and was against the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a republic, that it opposed the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina that would put it on equal footing with the rest of the republics. Can you tell us what did the SDS leadership do in the months following the elections and especially on the eve of the war of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party, after the elections, and seeking support from Belgrade, endeavoured to create a State within a State in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It developed a relationship with the JNA, and was one of the political actors in the preparation for the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They started establishing in Bosnia-Herzegovina wherever there was a Serbian population or wherever there was a Serbian majority -- they started establishing the independent autonomous regions. Five such autonomous regions were formed in 1991. After that an assembly of the Serbian people was established in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which adopted several decisions on further build-up of political structures of Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. After these Serbian autonomous regions -- Serbian municipalities are being established. These municipalities were supposed to be established in two kinds of ways. According to one, it would be where the Serbs formed a majority within the territory or municipality and, also, where there was Serbian minority within a municipality, they also formed their own Serbian municipality. All these together were to form a unified Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Also, SDS announced a programme how the Serbian people should act in a crisis situation, and this was adopted both in the municipalities with the Serb majority and minority. The plan was to, first of all, establish all structures of power, to organise self-defence, and that all these municipalities join according to a plan, which I have provided as a document, and there are further documents that give specific details of how this territorial expansion was going to take place. All this was done in secrecy, that is, wherever the Serbian population was in a minority, this process went on secretly, and, in secret, local boards were established. There were municipal boards and then they created further institutions -- committees and advisory boards -- and it went down to the local commune levels and everybody had their own tasks to organise people -- first, to organise watches, to control communication lines, to control the traffic of goods and such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are saying the same thing what Dr. Calic told us. Do you not think the statement is sufficient for that part of your case, Mr.s Residovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is possible that one part of the expert report coincides with the findings of Dr. Calic's report. However, there are parts which are different and this is why we felt the need to provide our own expert's opinion on the same topics. Professor, you said that in the period of 1991, the SDS implemented the plan of ethnic homogenisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in secret. Can you tell me, did the representatives of SDS go public with respect to these intentions at some point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was, by now, a notorious appearance of the President of the Serbian Democratic Party, Radovan Karadzic, in the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you comment on this, could we please ask the technical booth to play us tape marked 1, which is a part of the video material on which you based your expert report. Could we please have the technical booth run tape clip number 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, could you tell us what was the goal of this message of Radovan Karadzic -- how do you see it as an expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I think that it was to serve as attempt to dissuade the Parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina from proclaiming independence and I think, secondly, it was a warning to the Serbian population as to what they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have seen a short excerpt from the video material provided by Mr. Hadzibegovic's testimony. I would like now to tender this particular excerpt into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the evidence you want to tender -- the videotape?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The speech of Radovan Karadzic in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 14 October and I want to tender it as the basis and as a foundation for the expert opinion and I think that the relevance of this material is incontrovertible in light of the subsequent developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You might as well attempt to, but I do not know how you got the tape -- how did you get the tape?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The professor laid the ground and provided information on this piece of material. I think the professor quoted all the sources which it came from. A professor is a witness of those days. He is also a historian and this also served as a basis for his research and I believe that it is relevant to the events that are the matter of these proceedings anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is relevant to what he has been talking about -- I do not dispute that. Did he make the tape? How did he get it? Is it his own tape himself, or did he produce it? How was it produced?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have tried to explain -- I think this is an original tape from the TV Sarajevo and I think it was provided to us by the Institute for Research of War Crimes, and this is how it was provided to us. The professor was also a witness to this particular period -- the professor is a witness of the speech, as we were all at that time. The TV outlets around the world showed this. Your Honours, this excerpt has been introduced in the Tadic case already, and I think that, given that it concerns Dr. Karadzic, I think that it is relevant to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It depends on how it is introduced -- who did it and who makes the claim and these are the areas for introducing it. It is admissible, I do not deny that -- it is relevant but it depends on through whom it is introduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to Article 89, you are admitting it into evidence -- is that my correct understanding of what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If this witness claims to have produced the videotape itself and was also a witness to what happened, obviously he could himself tender it, if he made such claims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, were you a witness of this speech of Radovan Karadzic as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo when this took place and I was a witness of it, not only of what happened. At that time we did not have electricity, so I could not see it, but during the period of time when we did have electric power, we were able to see this -- it was rerun and it was a speech that shocked the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If a President of a Party which has no links to both Belgrade and the JNA, and that the JNA had overrun Bosnia -- we were all shocked, and very soon, on 6 April, when independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed, I was present when the people in the streets were shot at. I was a witness of the sniping of the people and this is what happened after this speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As I said, it is not that you were not a witness of it being run, but that is a different thing from producing a videotape itself. I agree -- you said it was submitted to you by the Institute -- a member of the Institute who took the videotape. He is a member of the Institute from which it has come, and introducing it as such from the Institute -- that is a different matter -- unless that is the basis on which he is doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness provided the tape as part of his research. It is not a tape that was given to the witness by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is acceptable, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us what the exhibit number is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit will be marked Defence Exhibit D141/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it one of those tendered for identification -- there are three tapes you tendered for identification -- D138 to D140. Does it belong to that group?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it belongs to that group, on my understanding, but I do not know which one of these and I do not know if these videotapes are the other exhibits. I prefer to give it a separate number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I need to remind you of the time. I do not know if this would be a good moment to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is a good point to stop, but, in addition to that, before we resume tomorrow, we would like to continue in a closed session for a status conference so we know exactly how things will be for the rest of the period. We will come back in five minutes now for a closed session and then carry on in a status conference tonight. 12

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 5.28 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 31st day of March, 1998 at 10 a.m.
